title: Valuing customers
harvard_reference: Gupta, S., Lehmann, D.R. and Stuart, J.A. (2004) 'Valuing customers', Journal of Marketing Research, 41(1), pp. 7-18. doi:10.1509/jmkr.41.1.7.25084.
abstract_summary: The authors argue that a firm's financial value increasingly depends on intangible assets, above all its customers. They define customer value as the expected sum of discounted future earnings from customers and show that valuing the customer base makes it feasible to value firms, including high-growth firms with negative earnings. Applying the method to publicly available data for five firms, they find that a 1% improvement in retention, margin, or acquisition cost improves firm value by about 5%, 1% and 0.1% respectively, and that retention has almost five times the impact on firm value of a 1% change in discount rate or cost of capital. They conclude that linking marketing concepts to shareholder value is both possible and insightful.

claims_supported.claim: A one-percentage-point improvement in retention increases customer value by a much larger amount (around 5 %) than a one-point improvement in margin or acquisition cost, so retention has high leverage on firm value.
claims_supported.where: Abstract (OpenAlex record of the JMR article): 'They find that a 1% improvement in retention, margin, or acquisition cost improves firm value by 5%, 1%, and .1%, respectively. They also find that retention has almost five times greater impact on firm value than a 1% change in discount rate or capital.' The full paper reports these sensitivities in its results/discussion of the five-firm application (Table on the impact of marketing and financial instruments on customer value). Two wording caveats: (a) the abstract says '1% improvement', not 'one percentage point'; mirror the paper's '1%' wording to be strictly faithful. (b) The abstract phrases the 5%/1%/0.1% effects as changes in FIRM value (derived from customer value, which the paper defines as the discounted sum of future customer earnings); the report should say 'firm value' or 'customer/firm value' rather than only 'customer value'.
